label: Side by Side
title: Dort, the Remonstrance and Molinism on the five disputed points
intro: The five points of Calvinism began as the Synod of Dort's answer to the five articles of the Remonstrants in 1610. Molinism adds a different question: what God knows about the free choices people would make. Each column follows its own source.
image_title: Calvinist, Arminian and Molinist answers to the five points
image_subtitle: The Synod of Dort (1618 to 1619), the Remonstrance (1610) and William Lane Craig, each in its own terms.
image_subtitle_narrow: Dort (1618 to 1619), the Remonstrance (1610) and William Lane Craig, each in its own terms.
image_source: Sources: Canons of Dort; Five Arminian Articles (1610); William Lane Craig, Reasonable Faith Q&A 79, 482
caption: All three hold that no one comes to God without his grace. They part over whether election rests on foreseen faith, for whom Christ died, whether grace can be resisted, and whether a believer can fall away.

rows.label: Can a sinner turn to God unaided?

cells.text: No. Without the Spirit's grace, people are neither willing nor able to return to God
cells.short: No: neither willing nor able without the Spirit

cells.text: No. Of themselves they cannot think, will or do anything truly good, saving faith included
No. Apart from God's grace no one can come to God
cells.short: No: not apart from God's grace

cells.text: Unconditional: a definite number chosen in Christ, not on the basis of foreseen faith
cells.short: Unconditional, not based on foreseen faith

cells.text: God decreed to save those who would believe in Christ and persevere in faith
cells.short: God chose to save those who believe and persevere

cells.text: Chiefly corporate: God chose a people, those who trust Christ; he knows who would freely respond
cells.short: Corporate: a people, those who trust Christ

cells.text: His death is sufficient for the whole world, but effectively redeems the elect only
cells.short: Sufficient for all; effective for the elect

cells.text: For all and for every one, though only believers enjoy the forgiveness he won
cells.short: For all; only believers receive it

cells.text: A payment sufficient for anyone's sins, which each must receive by faith
cells.short: Sufficient for anyone; received by faith

cells.text: No. God regenerates without our help; it is not left in human power
cells.short: No: God regenerates without our help

cells.text: Yes. Grace begins all good, but it is not irresistible
Yes. All receive sufficient grace; some freely resist it
cells.short: Yes: sufficient grace can be resisted

cells.text: No. God preserves true believers to the end
Left open in 1610: to be settled from Scripture first
Middle knowledge does not settle it; Molinists differ

common_text: All three begin with grace: Dort, the Remonstrants and Craig agree that no fallen person comes to God without it. Craig also quotes the Westminster Confession's statement that God ordains whatever comes to pass without taking away the liberty of the creature, and says, "Now this is precisely what the Molinist believes!"
differ: Election: Dort says God chose for the purpose of faith, not because of foreseen faith; the Remonstrants tie election to those who would believe and persevere.
Atonement: all three call Christ's death enough for anyone. Dort says it effectively redeems the elect only; the Remonstrants and Craig say it is received by faith.
Grace: the Remonstrants and Craig say it can be resisted; Dort says regeneration is not left in human power.
Molinism's own claim is about God's knowledge: he knows what each person would freely do in any circumstance and orders the world with that knowledge.
Molinism is not a full five point system. Craig says middle knowledge could even be paired with a limited atonement.
note: Cells paraphrase each source; the perseverance cell for Molinism draws on Craig's Q&A 482 and Philip Congdon's 2019 paper. No view is presented here as the answer.

sources.publisher: Christian Reformed Church in North America
sources.title: Canons of Dort
sources.quote: This same election took place, not on the basis of foreseen faith, of the obedience of faith, of holiness, or of any other good quality and disposition
sources.notes: Synod met "in the city of Dordrecht in 1618-19" (page intro). Rows: depravity (III/IV Art. 3: "neither willing nor able to return to God"), election (I.7, I.9), atonement (II.3 "more than sufficient to atone for the sins of the whole world"; II.8 "all those and only those who were chosen"), grace (III/IV Art. 12 "which God works in us without our help"), perseverance (V.3, V.8 "with respect to God it cannot possibly happen").

sources.title: The Five Arminian Articles, A.D. 1610 (Philip Schaff, Creeds of Christendom, Vol. III)
sources.quote: But as respects the mode of the operation of this grace, it is not irresistible, inasmuch as it is written concerning many, that they have resisted the Holy Ghost.
sources.notes: Art. I "those who, through the grace of the Holy Ghost, shall believe on this his Son Jesus, and shall persevere in this faith"; Art. II "died for all men and for every man ... yet that no one actually enjoys this forgiveness of sins except the believer"; Art. III "That man has not saving grace of himself, nor of the energy of his free will"; Art. V "that must be more particularly determined out of the Holy Scripture, before we ourselves can teach it".

sources.title: Molinism and Divine Election (Q&A 79)
sources.quote: God knows in exactly what circumstances people will freely respond to His grace and places people in circumstances in which each one receives sufficient grace for salvation if only that person will avail himself of it.
sources.notes: October 20, 2008. Also: "John 6. 65 means that apart from God's grace no one can come to God on his own." "Election, then, is first and foremost a corporate notion: God has chosen for Himself a people". "some persons freely resist God's grace". Rows: depravity, election, grace.

sources.title: Limited Atonement (Q&A 482)
sources.quote: It is as if Christ has made a massive downpayment sufficient to pay for anyone's sins, which we must then appropriate in order to become a beneficiary.
sources.notes: July 11, 2016. Also: "Via middle knowledge, we could, if we wanted, combine a doctrine of limited atonement with the universal availability of salvation." Rows: atonement, perseverance (Molinism as such leaves room), differ bullet 5.

sources.title: Molinism vs. Calvinism (Q&A 157)
sources.quote: Now this is precisely what the Molinist believes!
sources.notes: April 19, 2010. Said of Westminster Confession III.1, which he quotes in full.

sources.title: A Free Grace Response to Keathley's Molinist Soteriology (Philip F. Congdon)
sources.quote: not all Molinists would agree with his five points
sources.notes: Said of Kenneth Keathley's ROSES (a Molinist restatement of the five points). Supports the Molinist perseverance cell: Molinists differ on the five points. Congdon writes from a Free Grace view, not as a Molinist.

sources.title: Molinism 101 (Paul Helm)
sources.quote: God knows what they would freely choose in every possible circumstance.
sources.notes: A Reformed critic's definition of middle knowledge, used for differ bullet 4. Not used as a Molinist voice.
